demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
She is 38, a Latin American woman who has spent most of her adult life working long shifts in a factory that packages food for distribution. Before the loss, her life sounds narrow but steady. She wakes before dawn, ties her hair back, catches the bus with the same women from her neighborhood, and works beside the loud conveyor belts for hours at a time. She is single and lives with her younger brother for several years after their mother dies. In the way she tells it, he is the one person who makes the apartment feel warm. He cooks on Sundays, leaves music playing in the kitchen, and waits up for her when she comes home late from overtime. She describes him as “the one who always answered.”

The traumatic event happens on an ordinary weekday. She is midway through a shift, wearing gloves and ear protection, when her phone keeps vibrating in the pocket of her apron. She ignores it at first because the line supervisor dislikes interruptions. When she finally steps away and checks the screen, she sees missed calls from a neighbor, then from an unknown number. A police officer tells her there has been an accident. Her brother has been hit by a car while crossing an intersection near their apartment. By the time she reaches the hospital, breathless and still in her work uniform, he is already dead.

She returns to that afternoon over and over, not as a memory she can place in the past, but as something that keeps happening to her. She says she still hears the rattle of the machines and feels her phone buzzing against her hip. Sometimes at work, when metal parts strike each other or a forklift backfires, her body jerks before she understands where she is. She sees the hospital hallway in flashes: the polished floor, the smell of disinfectant, the doctor’s mouth moving before she can understand the words. At night she dreams that her brother is calling and she cannot reach him, or that she is the one crossing the street and a car is coming fast toward her. She wakes with her heart racing, already alert, as if something terrible is in the room.

In the first months after his death, she tries to continue as before. She goes back to the factory because missing work means risking rent money, but she begins to move through her days like someone bracing for impact. She avoids the intersection where he was killed, even if that means taking a longer bus route and arriving late. She cannot pass the hospital without turning her face to the window. She stops answering calls from unfamiliar numbers because the sound of the ringtone makes her stomach drop. If her phone rings repeatedly, her hands start shaking.

At home, the apartment no longer feels like a place to rest. She keeps his bedroom door closed, then feels guilty for closing it. Some evenings she opens it and stands there looking at his shoes lined up neatly by the wall, his jacket still hanging behind the door, and she feels both pulled toward the room and unable to step inside. She tells herself she should sort through his things, but every attempt ends with her sitting on the floor crying so hard she cannot catch her breath. She sleeps on the couch instead of in her bed because from there she can see the front door. She checks the lock several times each night. She says she knows, rationally, that no one is coming in, but her body does not believe what her mind says.

At work she becomes quieter. Coworkers notice she startles easily and drops items when someone approaches from behind. When the line jams and the alarm sounds, she feels heat rush through her body and has to step into the bathroom to splash water on her face. She begins volunteering for tasks that keep her away from loading docks and traffic noise. During lunch breaks she sits alone, scrolling through old text messages from her brother, rereading simple things—“Did you eat?” “I’m making rice tonight”—until the screen blurs. She used to joke with the women on her shift; now she keeps her head down because she is afraid that if anyone asks how she is, she will either say nothing or never stop crying.

She speaks of guilt as if it has weight. She wonders why she did not answer the first call, why she was at work while he was alone, why she did not insist he take a taxi that day though she had no way of knowing what would happen. She knows these thoughts do not make sense, yet they return whenever she is still. To avoid them, she keeps the television on all evening and falls asleep to the noise. On weekends, when there is too much silence, she cleans compulsively or takes extra shifts. Crowds make her tense, but being alone feels worse.

Now, more than a year later, she says life has divided into “before” and “after.” She still goes to the factory, still catches the early bus, still folds her uniform at night, but nearly everything is organized around preventing the next shock. She scans intersections before crossing, even on footpaths with no cars. She calls people repeatedly if they are late answering. She rarely makes plans and does not let herself imagine the future clearly. The world feels fragile and easily broken. She misses her brother in the smallest moments—seeing a recipe he would have liked, hearing a song from the kitchen radio, reaching for her phone at the end of a hard shift and remembering there is no one waiting to answer.
